title: A Tradition You Have Not Seen

items.prompt: Predict the order of these stages of Bagru hand block printing.

options.label: Mordant printing (chhapai) with syahi and begar
Yellow over-dyeing by sponging (haldi-naspal putai / potai)

config.account:
Bagru hand block printing is a tradition you have not seen. These are its stages, in no particular order.
Mordant printing (chhapai) with syahi and begar: The fabric is printed with two mordants: ferrous syahi from rusted horseshoe nails, and aluminium sulphate begar.
Resist printing with dabu (dabu chhapai)
Washing off excess mordant (khulai)
Final washing (dhulai) and finishing
Alum after-mordanting (fitkari rangai)
Yellow over-dyeing by sponging (haldi-naspal putai / potai)
Scouring (hari sarana / teluni): Scouring, locally 'hari sarana', removes starch, oil and dust; cloth was left overnight in cow dung and water.
Indigo dyeing (neel rangai): The cloth is folded like sari pleats, lowered into the tank, and each pleat opened under the liquid so dye reaches evenly.
Harda treatment (peela karna)
Dyeing in alizarin/madder (rangai, bhatti): The dye reacts with two mordants at two locations on the same print, giving red (with alum) and black (with ferrous).
Ageing / drying (sukhai): Printed fabric is left at least three to four days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre; the longer the ageing, the better the result.

title: A Tradition You Have Not Seen

items.prompt: Which stage comes straight after Sun-drying the resist?

config.account:
Dabu mud-resist block printing is a tradition you have not seen. These are its stages, in no particular order.
Dip-dyeing (usually indigo)
Dusting the wet resist: Paste areas are immediately covered with sawdust to prevent smudging.
Washing / scouring the cloth
Collecting and soaking the mud: Mud is dug from a dry pond and soaked overnight in a separate tank.
Airing and drying
Preparing the resist paste
Optional pre-printing of colour (naphthol red)
Repeating resist-dye cycles (double/triple dabu)
Block-printing the resist: Craftsmen dip the blocks into a viscous paste of mud, gum and lime; the method's name comes from dabaana, to press.
Sun-drying the resist
Washing off the resist: The fabric is washed to remove paste and excess dye.
